turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: I’m here because I can’t stop noticing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face, especially in the lesson videos. Once I see it, I just feel like the students, parents, and staff must be staring at that instead of hearing anything I’m saying.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with a perceived crooked, swollen-looking side of their face and concern that others are staring at it.

turns.doctor_question: Have family members, friends, or anyone else noticed or commented on this swelling, or do they see it differently?
turns.patient_response: I can’t stop seeing it myself, especially on the lesson videos. It looks crooked and swollen to me, and I just assume everyone watching is focused on that instead of what I’m teaching.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports persistent preoccupation with a perceived crooked, swollen appearance of one side of their face, especially when viewing lesson videos, and believes others focus on it.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself spending a lot of time repeatedly checking your face in mirrors or on your screen?
turns.patient_response: Yes. Before I post a lesson or join a parent conference, I keep adjusting the camera angle and replaying the video over and over. I’ll cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks better, and sometimes I re-record the whole thing so many times that I miss prep work and end up late for class.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient reports repeatedly adjusting the camera angle, replaying videos, covering parts of their face, and re-recording lessons due to appearance concerns, causing lateness and missed preparation work.
